Apple's lawsuit against OpenAI over trade secrets has been reassigned to U.S. District Judge Edward Davila, replacing the magistrate judge originally assigned to handle the case. Here are the details.

New judge takes over, October hearing cancelled

When civil lawsuits are filed in the Northern District of California, cases are randomly assigned to a U.S. district judge or a magistrate judge. If a case is assigned to a magistrate judge, all parties must indicate whether they consent to that judge handling the case in its entirety.

This is because U.S. district judges have the authority to oversee federal civil cases throughout, while magistrate judges can only do so with the consent of all parties.

On the day Apple filed suit against two former employees, OpenAI, and Jony Ive's io Products, the case was randomly assigned to Magistrate Judge Virginia K. DeMarchi.

This means all parties involved in the litigation needed to submit forms indicating whether they consented to DeMarchi handling the case in its entirety.

Apple appears to have indicated refusal. The company filed a consent or refusal declaration yesterday (not yet publicly available), which appears to have triggered the process of reassigning the case to a U.S. district judge.

There currently appear to be no other documents explaining this reassignment, strongly suggesting that Apple checked the option on the form refusing to accept the magistrate judge's jurisdiction.

Accordingly, the case has now been reassigned to U.S. District Judge Edward Davila, with Magistrate Judge Nathanael Cousins handling discovery matters.

With the case reassigned, the initial case management conference previously scheduled for October 13 before Judge DeMarchi has been cancelled and must be rescheduled before Judge Davila.

However, two other sets of deadlines remain in effect: parties must meet by September 22 to discuss settlement and discovery plans, and submit initial disclosure and joint case management statements by October 6.
